refactory/docs/concepts.md.text:
# Concepts

Refactory makes an agentic workflow explicit, interactive and searchable. A mode can be small or elaborate: research and QA are graph choices, not requirements imposed on every harness.

![The mode and artifact workflows](assets/refactory-flow.svg)

## Packages, modes and Tasks

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Package** | A named collection of Python modes and their supporting operations |
| **Mode** | An explicit graph, declared knobs and input/output contracts; a scored mode also defines the objective used by optimization |
| **Task** | The source of work items, per-item preparation and verification used by a mode's data node |
| **CEO** | The conversational coordinator that drives the graph and delegates its agent nodes |
| **Outer loop** | A search that proposes, validates and measures permitted changes to a mode |

Shipped packages live in `refactory/refactory_packages/`. Created, imported and adopted packages live in the project's `.factory/packages/`. Both use the same registry. A package may be disabled without deleting it.

Create produces a reusable package; Edit produces a revised package and records where it came from. Both stage their output in a per-run directory inside the run (`<run>/.factory-staging/.factory/packages/<name>/`), so two parallel runs of the same package name never collide; at registration the staged package is copied atomically to the shared `.factory/packages/<name>/` (write a sibling directory, rename the old aside, rename the new in, then delete the old), and the copy is refused — naming the other run — if the shared package's state differs from what prepare recorded, including when it now exists but did not before. A git worktree is not used because `.factory/` is gitignored: a worktree of the project contains no `.factory/packages/`, and nothing written there becomes a commit. The per-run staging directory isolates the run, and `prepare_create()` records both `source_hash` and `source_existed` so `register()` detects all conflicts. After a successful register, the origin stamp in `.origin.json` identifies the registering run so a reloop does not refuse itself. Design produces software: commits on its own branch, in a git worktree of the repository it changes or of a new project in `~/refactory-projects/` (a run with its worktree off writes `.factory/artifacts/` instead). A Design run whose reviews pass delivers that branch as a pull request, which its approval gate names first; design_fast, which has no approval gate, leaves it on the branch. When a limit stops a Design run's build loop (the check, review, overall attempts or refusal limit) at an applied commit with current check evidence, that commit is delivered as a draft PR whose description lists what is unresolved first, marked `[check failing]` when its check fails; any other stop still ends the run with no PR. The `draft_delivery` fact carries the reason and the unresolved items. Any mode that changes a repository can take the same steps: see [if your mode changes a repository](tutorials/01-write-a-mode.md#if-your-mode-changes-a-repository). Create, create_fast, edit and edit_fast also isolate their writes; see the [mode classification table](#mode-classification-table) below. Create and Design are deliberately unscored authoring modes: successful completion is governed by their graph's checks, not a numeric search objective. Standalone Design artifacts are not optimizer candidates.

### Mode classification table

| Mode | Writes today | Isolation method |
|---|---|---|
| design | worktree at `~/.refactory/worktrees/` (via `repo_change.locate`) | git worktree |
| design_fast | worktree at `~/.refactory/worktrees/` (via `repo_change.locate`) | git worktree |
| create | `.factory/packages/<name>/` via per-run staging, then copy-on-register | staging directory |
| create_fast | `.factory/packages/<name>/` via per-run staging, then copy-on-register | staging directory |
| edit | `.factory/packages/<name>/` via per-run staging, then copy-on-register | staging directory |
| edit_fast | `.factory/packages/<name>/` via per-run staging, then copy-on-register | staging directory |
| loop | `.factory/loop/<run-id>/` (run directory only) | none needed |
| optimize | `.factory/loop/<run-id>/` (run directory only) | none needed |

## What a graph contains

| Node | Work |
|---|---|
| `op` | Invoke a Python operation |
| `agent` | Delegate a tool-using agent task; it can involve multiple model turns |
| `gate` | Route on a deterministic, agent or user verdict |
| `fork` / `join` | Dispatch independent branches and wait for their results |
| `data` | Run a subgraph over a Task's items |

Nodes declare inputs, outputs and facts. Runtime validation catches structural violations; the mode's own checks establish its application requirements. Neither a file's existence nor an agent's statement proves its content correct.

A user gate is an explicit control point. The runtime asks the person or uses their deliberately configured authorization; the coordinator cannot invent approval.

## Graph execution and interactivity

The CLI and GUI present the same underlying workflows. The CEO uses workflow tools to open a graph, see the due node, dispatch workers and record completion. The runtime owns the cursor and the gates. Its guard disables the CEO's direct coding and skill tools during graph execution.

Workers may use skills as supporting instructions. The graph's structure and durable run state remain the execution mechanism. A graph does not depend on an agent remembering a checklist in a skill document.

Steering notes are recorded and supplied to subsequent work. Explicit prompt edits and reruns change a selected node's execution. Notes do not automatically rewrite deterministic operations, and delivery does not prove semantic compliance. See [Terminal and GUI](interfaces.md) for the current timing and UI boundaries.

## State, knobs and protected requirements

A Python mode declares its initial graph with `build()`. After that, `state_dict()` contains the graph and knobs as serializable data. The optimizer edits this state; it does not rewrite `build()` or arbitrary source files.

Knobs are declared inputs and parameters with types, bounds and mutability. Use them to pass actual values into deterministic operations. An intent such as “count to twenty” is context; `target=20` supplies the input.

A scored mode's `score()` and `invariants()` are methods outside the editable state. The validator enforces those declared boundaries before evaluating proposals. Required artifacts that are not part of a numeric score need meaningful invariants and acceptance checks; a higher score alone does not establish that every user requirement survived.

## The configurable outer loop

Three choices are independent:

| Choice | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| **Strategy / outer loop** | Organize selection, proposal rounds and stopping |
| **Optimizer** | Propose candidate edits |
| **Evaluator** | Execute a candidate and measure its result |

The default walker evaluates the graph in Python and supplies a model client to agent nodes. The DSH evaluator lowers the graph and runs it through the shipping DSH runtime. Both carry the run's selected model/worker context to agent nodes; see [Models](models.md#model-selection-across-execution-paths).

Permitted edits can include knobs, prompts, nodes and edges, subject to the selected preset and invariants. A proposal is validated before it can spend candidate evaluation budget. Execution failures are recorded but cannot win.

For Task-bound modes, candidates use the training partition and the winner is audited on held-out items. A mode without a data split reports holdout as not applicable. The compared score can include a graph-size penalty; the raw score is retained separately.

A [profile](optimization-profiles.md) versions the search settings and objective; each run retains its own resolved snapshot. Opt-in repeats report actual trial count and variability, while shared budgets account for proposals, evaluations and validation. Adoption writes the exact eligible winner into a new package with its profile and audit provenance. It does not alter the source package or guarantee a future stochastic run will reproduce the same outputs. No-improvement searches are valid outcomes.

## Models, agents and runtimes

Cordis supplies plugin composition and service lifecycle. DSH supplies the current agent runtime, tools, sessions and model-provider adapters. Refactory supplies modes, graph execution/steering and the meta outer loop.

The model provider and coding-agent runtime are different choices. Today, choosing an OpenAI model still runs the DSH coding agent. Optional Codex and Claude Code workers require an explicit backend selection and their native setup; they are not enabled by a model-name change. [Worker capabilities](models.md#model-provider-versus-coding-agent) define the supported controls.

## What evidence means

Keep three questions separate:

1. Did the framework execute the declared graph and handle gates, steering, failure and cleanup correctly?
2. Did the artifact meet its declared acceptance checks?
3. How good was the model's output across the workload, and at what cost?

A checker can be too narrow, a valid workflow can generate a poor answer, and a model timeout can leave a correctly reported failed run. Preserve the exact result and use the appropriate measurements for each question.

Next: [get started](getting-started.md), [write a mode](tutorials/01-write-a-mode.md), [Tasks](datasets.md), or [architecture](architecture.md).

refactory/docs/contributing.md.text:
# Contributing

For anyone — person or coding agent — changing `refactory/`. It assumes you have
read [the architecture overview](architecture.md), and it is about the rules that
are not visible from the code alone: which invariants must hold, what will break
if you move something, and how to check your work.

## The commands

Run from the repository root.

```bash
uv run python -m pytest refactory/tests/ -q                    # the suite
uv run python -m pytest refactory/tests/ -q -n 4               # ... on four workers (22.4 min to 5.7 min)
uv run python -m pytest refactory/tests/ -q --run-integration  # ... plus the real-DSH runs

`-n` is a command-line choice, not a setting: `--toolchain-gate` must stay in one process
(it refuses `-n` rather than passing a suite it did not check), and the per-site base
check runs a single test under a time cap.
uv run python -m refactory_dsh.tools.gen_api_reference --check # docs match the code
uv sync --group reference                                      # add the test-time oracle
```

`tests/test_ir_parity.py` compares `refactory_dsh/ir.py` with the reference graph
language over every shipped mode. That reference is a **test-time oracle** and not
a runtime dependency: it lives in the non-default `reference` group. CI installs it
so the parity tests run on every pull request; a local `uv sync --group reference`
adds it for development.

The DSH side, when you touch `packages/`:

```bash
pnpm run build                 # typecheck, then the host and client bundle passes
pnpm run test                  # the eight packages' vitest suites
pnpm run lint                  # oxlint
pnpm run typecheck
```

The gates the harness copy carried are gone with it. [Verification](verification.md)
names what replaced each one, what a contributor runs before pushing, and what is not
covered.

`.work/todo.json` tracks the work, and `tests/test_work_complete.py` **fails while
any item is open**. Each item records its issue number, the command that verifies
it, and the observed result; that test also checks the command names files that
exist, because two items once named test files that never existed and nobody
noticed.

## The environment, and what it hides

**Lean and mathlib are optional, and their absence is silent.** The Lean tests skip when `lean` is not on `PATH`; the mathlib tests skip when `MATHLIB_PATH` is unset. A skipped test cannot fail, so a green suite on a machine without them says nothing about the checker path — which is how two real defects hid. Every test that exercises a real external tool is marked `toolchain`, and one command reports which ran, which skipped and why, and fails if any did not run:

```bash
uv run python -m pytest refactory/tests -q --toolchain-gate
```

No per-PR job installs Lean or mathlib (mathlib is a 7.4 GB checkout, and this suite is not in the DSH CI matrix), so those paths are verified on developer machines by that gate. A machine without the tools is expected to fail it and to say what it did not verify.

**A DSH profile is machine state, not a checkout artifact.** It is created with `dsh plugin --profile <name> add <package>`. This checkout owns two: `graph`, which the Python glue runs modes on, and `refactory`, which the GUI boots over the harness's own `web` template — the harness's `web` profile is never written to, so a plain `dsh --profile web` session shows no re:factory rows. `refactory` needs both the `ceo` preset layer and the web-surface layer — without the preset every session it creates without naming one stops, and without the surface the console and picker rows never mount. `install.sh` provisions both idempotently, `./refactory-dsh` heals a missing layer before booting, and `REFACTORY_SKIP_DSH_PROFILE=1` skips both. `refactory_dsh/dsh_profile.py` is the one place that answers "is the profile there, does it point to this checkout, and what fixes it" — it owns the layer and target tables, emits the `init`/`add`/`remove` plan the installer and the launcher execute, and detects a harness profile an old install mutated; `refactory doctor`, the runner and the tests all read it. The profile links to one checkout at a time. A run from a different checkout (a second clone, a worktree, a contributor's branch) will refuse and name the `dsh plugin` command that relinks the profile. A contributor working from a second checkout must relink or re-run `install.sh`. Martty is an **attached** target: the operator adds the preset layer to the profile they already have, and re:factory never creates it. Without the profile, anything that runs a mode on DSH stops at the first call.

**`install.sh` provisions the default install, not the optional parts.** It creates
`.venv` from `uv.lock`'s default (`dev`) group and installs the pinned pnpm workspace
with the eight packages' `lib/` built, then creates the DSH profiles above. It does
**not** install the non-default `reference` group — the parity oracle, added with
`uv sync --group reference` — and it does not create `refactory/vendor/srf/graphs`,
the legacy graph directory for the low-level `dsh --profile graph run` path; the
public `uv run refactory ceo <package>/<mode>` route supplies its own graph directory.
`.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs `install.sh` for the default install, then adds the
reference group so the IR parity tests run on every pull request; the reference stays
out of the default install.

**Use managed credentials for nested model execution.** Save the provider key through **Settings → Models → Edit → API key → Apply** in the DSH home used by the run. Exported keys and repository `.env` can serve the launching process, but nested smoke deliberately scrubs credential environment variables and changes `HOME`; the product carries the nonsecret DSH-home location so DSH can resolve its managed store. See [Models](models.md#credentials-for-nested-execution) for precedence and setup, and use `refactory doctor --provider deepseek-official --model deepseek-flash` to check downstream configuration before authoring. This check does not authenticate the key; unsupported custom runtimes report an explicit unverified warning. Deterministic modes, searches with `--optimizer random`, and offline tests do not need model credentials.

## The invariants

These are the rules the system is built on. Breaking one is not a style problem;
each exists because its absence caused a specific failure.

### The state is the authority after genesis

`build()` runs **once**, to produce the starting state. Every later architecture
comes from the state dict, because that is what the optimizer edits.

- Never read a knob's value in `build()`. A knob is consumed by a node at run time.
- Never make `build()` depend on I/O, the clock, or randomness — it must be pure,
  or `build() -> state -> build()` stops being an identity.
- `score()` and `invariants()` are **methods**, never state. That is what makes
  them unreachable by a proposal, and it is the whole protection. Do not put them
  in the state dict, and do not make a candidate able to influence them.

### A candidate is judged before it costs anything

`Optimizer.attempt` applies and validates the edit *before* the loop evaluates
anything. A proposal that would produce an invalid graph costs no budget.

- A new rule goes in `nn/validate.py` and in the `RULES` table. `tests/test_integrity.py`
  asserts the table and the emitted codes are the same set **in both directions**,
  so a rule that is emitted but unpublished fails the suite.
- The validator **refuses; it never repairs.** A repair hides the edit that caused
  the problem and makes the next failure unattributable.
- Macros are literal compositions of primitives. If you add one, express it as an
  `expand` into primitives rather than as new application logic, or it can produce
  a state no sequence of primitives could.

### Every knob is reachable, and every file is produced

- `V7` refuses a declared knob no node consumes **and** a node consuming an
  undeclared knob. A knob that looks like a search axis and is not is worse than
  no knob: the search spends batches learning nothing.
- `V6` refuses a node reading a file no node on a start-to-terminal path writes.
- `V11` refuses a declared port no node writes.
- A `str` knob may be declared `required=True`. Its default is then only a
  placeholder: a run with no value for it (in its knobs or its task), or an empty
  or blank one, is refused before its run directory exists, naming the knob -- by
  `Mode.run`, and by `interactive.prepare` for a headless run. A session a person
  opens may start without it, since the value can come in the conversation; there
  only a value given explicitly blank is refused. V9, which validates a mode's
  structure and starting state, refuses only a blank value a candidate sets.
- `Loop.unreachable_knobs()` reports knobs that *this optimizer* cannot move even
  though they are declared and consumed. It warns rather than refuses, because a
  knob-only optimizer on a structural mode is a legitimate pairing.

### The journal is the only durable state

`journal.jsonl` is append-only and replayed. Do not add a second snapshot of the
population and keep it consistent by hand — that is what the system this replaced
did, and it produced real bugs.

- Anything a later step needs must be **journaled**, not derived. `generation`,
  `refusal_pressure`, and `bound` are all journaled for this reason: a resumed run
  that guessed them would take a different path.
- An invalid candidate is recorded as a `Rejection` with its reasons, never
  dropped in silence. `E-duplicate` exists because a silently dropped duplicate
  loses a batch slot and makes the run report a batch it did not try.

### The two runtimes must agree

The walker is a debug runtime; DSH ships. Two tests run the same thing both ways:

- `tests/test_equivalence.py` runs a deterministic mode on the walker and on a real DSH
  session and compares the score and facts (`--run-integration`, real model calls).
- `tests/test_runtime_equivalence.py` runs one scripted design run (a gate answered with
  a correction, a self-check fix-up, the reviews, a pull request) through each runtime's
  real entry point, and compares visits, verdicts, facts, run files, prompts, model routes,
  commits and the delivery.

Its known differences are named parity gaps (`GAPS`), each a strict xfail. When you
close one, remove it from `SCENARIO_GAPS` in the same change; a difference that no gap
explains fails the test.

- If you change the executor, change nothing that makes a node behave differently
  on DSH. The lowering in `lowering.py` is the seam, and `refactory_dsh/ir.py` owns
  the IR it lowers into. `tests/test_ir_parity.py` holds that copy against the
  reference over every shipped mode: the serialization is byte-identical, and the
  reference's validator accepts the result except for two modes whose refusal is a
  limit of that validator, both recorded in `REFERENCE_REFUSALS` there.
- The IR has **no field for the facts a node produces**, so `write_declarations`
  writes them beside the graph and the runner reads them from the run directory.
  That is a known wart, not an oversight to "clean up" silently.

## The failure modes worth remembering

Each of these happened, and the shape of the code is the response.

- **A severed gradient.** The optimizer was not shown what the run learned.
  `backward()` produces the gradient and it is part of the API; `knob_attribution`
  includes `untried`, because *a value that failed* and *a value nobody tried* are
  different facts and a prompt that conflates them keeps re-proposing what it
  already knows.
- **Mutating operators that destroyed graphs.** Some rewrites produced structures
  that could not run. Hence: macros expand to primitives, the validator refuses
  rather than repairs, and validation happens before budget is spent.
- **A surface that lied.** Structural wins were counted from failed runs, and
  duplicates vanished. `structural_wins` requires `exit_ok`; duplicates are refused
  at the optimizer layer and `attempt == 0` is asserted in the tests.
- **Steps that deleted their own run.** When the loop became a mode, each node
  rehydrates from the journal — and `resume=False` means "start over", so the
  first version deleted the journal between two nodes of the loop's own run. Any
  node that reads the run must resume.

## Where to put a change

| you want to | change |
|---|---|
| a new mode | a package under `refactory_packages/` |
| a new validator rule | `nn/validate.py` `RULES` + the check, then the anti-drift test |
| a new edit operation | `nn/edits.py`: a primitive, or a macro that expands to primitives |
| a new optimizer | subclass `optim.Optimizer`, implement `propose`, register it |
| a new outer loop | subclass `outerloop.OuterLoop`, override the steps |
| a new strategy | `strategies.py`; a port of an SRF mode |
| a new artifact | declare a `Port` on the mode **and** write it from a node |
| a new way to read a run | `observe.py` (readers) or `history.py` (finished runs) |
| the loop's own steps | `loop.py` — and expect `loop_mode/loop` to need matching changes |

## Documentation

- The [API reference](api/reference.md) is **generated**; never edit it. Run
  `uv run python -m refactory_dsh.tools.gen_api_reference`. `tests/test_docs_api.py`
  fails when it is stale, when a documented symbol has no prose, or when a
  document names a module that does not import.
- The architecture overview's rule table is checked against `nn.RULES`, so adding
  a rule means updating the overview too.
- Prose belongs in the overview and the tutorials. A comment belongs where the
  reason for the code is local to it.

## What not to do

- **Do not add a second runtime.** The walker is for debugging; DSH ships. A third
  executor is a third set of behaviours to keep in agreement.
- **Do not silently accept an invalid candidate** to keep a batch full.
- **Do not default a missing referent.** `Package` resolution refuses a bare mode
  name rather than guessing a package, and the registry refuses a name that exists
  in both roots rather than picking one.
- **Do not repair a state.** Refuse it and report the reason.

## Public capability coverage

See [discovery](discovery.md) for the shared parser/mode contract, semantic review
metadata, offline generation and extension checklist. Run `pnpm run docs:generate`
after reviewed changes and `pnpm run docs:check` before building. New public
operations, mode schemas and worker capabilities require current explanations,
examples and explicit CLI/chat/panel routes.

refactory/docs/datasets.md.text:
# Datasets and Tasks

A mode normally walks its graph once. A mode with a **`data` node** walks a subgraph
once per *item* — one benchmark instance, one row of a file, one directory — and an
item can carry its own prompt and its own verdict. That is how a benchmark or a
dataset becomes a mode instead of a script around one.

## A harness is for a class of work

What this system produces is a harness for a **class** of work — "write the build config for any Java buildroot", not "write the config for this buildroot". A mode that runs once is the special case rather than the default, because a mode that was tuned until one instance passed makes no claim about the next instance.

The `data` node is the harness's **input port**. What it is pointed at at run time — a bound Task's `instances()`, a directory, a JSONL or CSV file — is material rather than meaning, and a harness with its items written into the graph is a harness for exactly those items. `create` binds a Task by name and leaves the port open, and the validate gate refuses a package whose items are baked into the graph instead of read from the node at run time.

A class-of-work harness scores **per item**: its `score()` aggregates the verdicts the Task's `verify` returned for each pass, and the run reports the individual verdicts under the `item_scores` fact alongside that aggregate. That is what makes the score a statement about the class rather than about the one run that produced it.

## The node

```python
graph.add(nn.Node(
    "data", "data",
    subgraph_entry="work",     # the first node of the per-item subgraph
    subgraph_exit="work",      # the last one, included in every pass
    task_ref="my_pack.tasks:MyTask",   # where the items come from (optional)
    writes=("current_item.json",),
    produces=("item_scores",),
))
graph.connect("data", "finish")        # where the run goes after every item
```

The subgraph is reached **through the data node**, not by an edge: an edge into it
would run it once outside the iteration. Each pass writes the item to
`current_item.json` in the run directory, so an op or an agent node reads the item it
is working on rather than being told it in a prompt.

Items come from, in order of precedence: `inline_items` declared on the node; the
`source_path` read as `source_format` (`directory` — sorted subdirectories; `jsonl` —
one object per line; `csv` — a header row); or the bound Task's `instances()`. The
node's `limit` caps what is used. A source that is named and missing is refused by
name, because an empty selection and an unbound source must not look alike.

## Feeding it at run time

The graph declares the source the mode was built with, and a run may name another. That is what makes a harness usable on items it has never seen without editing the mode:

```bash
uv run refactory ceo java_build_pack/build --source /path/to/my/trees
```

The runner writes the choice into the run directory as `items.json`, and `load_items` reads it on both runtimes, so the walker and DSH iterate the same items. `--source-format` says how to read it (`directory` by default, or `jsonl`/`csv`), and an entry keyed `*` applies to every data node of the run while an entry keyed by node id wins for that node.

An item in a `directory` source is a subdirectory, and it may describe itself in an `item.json` beside its content — those fields reach the pass the way a Task's metadata does, which is how a harness learns an item's entry point. The directory's own name stays the id, so a described item cannot rename itself out of the selection it was listed in.

## The Task

A Task is three optional hooks, resolved by `module:Class` or by a name registered with
`register_task`. A reference that does not resolve is refused rather than run with
nothing judging the items.

```python
from refactory_dsh.task import Task, TaskInstance, VerifyResult

class CountingTask(Task):
    name = "counting"

    def instances(self):                      # the items
        return [TaskInstance(id="alpha"), TaskInstance(id="beta")]

    def setup(self, instance, workspace):     # before a pass
        ...

    def verify(self, instance, workspace):    # after a pass; None means "no opinion"
        return VerifyResult(passed=True, score=1.0)
```

There is no hook that writes the prompt. An item is data — it reaches the pass as `current_item.json` — and what the agent for an item is asked is the mode's own business, stated in its agent node's prompt template. Two places that both decide the ask is one place too many.

The verdicts are recorded as `item_scores` when the data node declares that fact, so
`score()` reads what the Task decided rather than a number the graph guessed.

## A worked example

A package with one data node bound to a two-item Task, whose subgraph is one op that
appends the current item's id, scores the mean of the Task's verdicts:

```bash
uv run refactory package smoke dataset_probe/dataset
```

```json
{"mode": "dataset_probe/dataset", "package": "dataset_probe", "exit_ok": true,
 "error": null, "score": 0.75, "iterations": 4}
```

`0.75` is the mean of `1.0` for `alpha` and `0.5` for `beta`: two passes, each with
its own item on disk, each judged by the Task.

A two-item Task proves the shape but not the claim. `java_build_pack` is the example that does the work the product is named for: its Task lists three small Java source trees, its one agent node writes `build.sh` for whichever item is on disk, and the Task runs that script and compares what the program printed with the output recorded beside the sources. The mode's score is the share of trees it built, and pointing the same harness at a fourth tree it has never seen is what the binding buys:

```bash
uv run refactory ceo java_build_pack/build --intent "build each Java tree the Task lists"
```

## Creating one

`create` makes you say which of the two things you are building, before it spends anything on a model:

```bash
# a harness for a class of work: the Task supplies the items and judges each pass
uv run refactory ceo "a harness that counts the items of any counting instance" \
  --mode create --name my_pack --task my_pack.tasks:CountingTask

# the special case: a harness for one run of one thing
uv run refactory ceo "a harness that counts to ten" --mode create --name my_once --single
```

Naming a Task is the whole directive: the produced package gets a `data` node bound to that Task, and the validate gate checks the package really has one rather than taking the prompt's word for it. A creation that names neither a Task nor `--single` is refused with both options named, because a harness built for one hardcoded example is the special case and must be asked for as one.

The validate gate refuses three shapes, each by name: a package that declares no data node when a Task was named, one whose data node is bound to a different Task, and one that closes its input port — items written into the graph as `inline_items`, or a data node that names neither a Task nor a source to read at run time. Asking is not the same as getting.

## On the runtimes

Both runtimes iterate the node the same way and produce the same facts. The walker
owns the whole loop and runs it in-process. DSH's spine walks the subgraph the way it
walks the rest of the graph, so the item loop is split across the loader's three
commands — `list` (how many items), `begin` (materialise one and run the Task's
`setup`), and `end` (run the Task's `verify` and record the score) — and each pass's
deterministic nodes run in-process while its agent nodes are handed to the subagents
the graph names. The loader is one implementation
(`refactory_dsh.nn.executor.load_items`), so the items a mode selects do not depend on
which runtime is running it. The composition supplies the command
(`dataCommand`, set by the `graph` bundle to `python -m refactory_dsh.items`); a graph
with a data node and no loader is refused at load rather than handed to the model,
because a model cannot enter a subgraph the cursor never enters.

`refactory/tests/test_equivalence.py` runs one data-driven mode on both runtimes and
compares the facts.

# CEO discovery and project-worker acceptance — 2026-09-27

This acceptance covers issues #253 and #254. It uses one new native CEO
conversation and one config-dispatched Codex worker. Existing adapter acceptance
in [release validation](release-validation-20260926.md) remains the evidence for
other backends; no three-backend or full-authoring campaign was repeated.

## Native run and identity

The run used the isolated `codex/ceo-discovery-project-workers` worktree based on
`8c3f2a61b738e8305e0d7b1ee10345b7deb91e3d`, with the implementation uncommitted.
Its returned build ID was
`3fe92e2189811c471ec44dae73e96ac644cff4f6e85935b40a82810c1759aaeb`;
documentation ID was
`188ca63a95177c6ace3e2d505551c714d963f050c0b9bcf0ef1791cf152ecbb9`.
Subsequent deterministic review fixes and reconciliation with merged authoring
changes change those IDs. This is evidence for the actual tested development
build, not a claim that a later commit ran another model acceptance.

The fixture `discovery_acceptance/worker_once` was installed after the build. It
has an `emit` agent (role `builder`) followed by a deterministic check requiring
`answer.txt` to contain exactly `42\n`. Live help listed it, including its missing
reviewed-guidance warnings. The project file contained:

```json
{"worker_backend":"dsh","node_routes":{"emit":{"worker_backend":"codex"}}}
```

The native CEO prompt required discovery through help, a mode-help read, a docs
search and page read, an effective-worker check, and one `wf_open` in a fresh
absolute work directory. It prohibited source archaeology, optimization, repair,
retry and out-of-graph delegation. No token cap was imposed. The CEO made ten
tool calls in eight steps: help, modes, mode help, docs search, workers, docs
page read, wf_open, wf_next, artifacts and wf_state. It used no shell, source
reader or web tool.

Session: `session-aa19f9b1-8682-4671-857c-db80ca251446`.
The CEO used the configured DeepSeek Flash selection. Summed assistant usage was
278,279 total tokens: 37,984 input, 238,080 cached input and 2,215 output;
643 reasoning tokens were reported within output. These figures are separate
from the native worker's usage.

Worker `worker-7c2827b6ce754da79d7d7729b4c61ef0` completed between
19:30:30.929 and 19:30:42.293 UTC. Its requested route was Codex with native
model/provider/effort selection and `skip` permissions. The actual native thread
reported `gpt-6-astra`, `openai`, `high`, Codex runtime `0.153.4`, adapter
`@deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent` `0.1.5-rc.3`, and 45,249 measured tokens. The measurement
excludes nested workers. There was one attempt. Independent file inspection and
`checked.json` verified exact `42\n` output.

## Terminal and panel

Public terminal calls read workers, mode help and the shipped routing page, then
prepared the same fixture with `console open --workdir <fresh-directory>`.
The generated node specification selected Codex from the same project map.
This was preparation evidence and did not launch a second model worker.

In native Chrome, the Modes panel selected the runtime-installed fixture. Its
**Mode help and effective project workers** disclosure returned the same mode,
build/docs identities and effective project defaults. Runtime controls showed
**Use project defaults**, inherited permission policy and no token limit.
Attaching the existing run showed finished/done, both nodes complete, the actual
Codex route and measured usage, and verified output facts. No second panel model
launch was claimed. Deterministic tests cover the shared preparation and panel
argument mapping.

The canonical `artifacts` list returned zero entries for the custom fixture's
noncanonical filenames. The graph's check, independent file inspection and panel
outputs established success; the CEO disclosed that artifact-list limitation.

## Checks and cleanup

Focused checks cover file/environment/profile/explicit precedence, backend
switches, role/node maps, invalid native fields, nested and saved-run isolation,
CLI/chat preparation, live package discovery, docs bounds and integrity, stale
coverage, broken links, generated chat-to-parser mappings and panel controls.
Final focused validation after reconciliation with main `364eeffc85` passed:

- 145 Python tests across discovery, project configuration, workers, interactive
  preparation, worker permissions, profiles, recovery and API docs.
- 164 TypeScript tests across the tool, generated invocation contract, profiles,
  body and steering ledger (including the independently merged panel changes).
- `pnpm run build`, including offline docs/coverage checks, host/client typechecks
  and both production bundles; normal commit/push hooks.

Exploratory wider runs also encountered existing failures. A detached baseline at
`3fd35ac7c9` reproduced two legacy graph-cycle assertions in `test_nn.py`, seven
service-mock failures in `service.spec.ts`, and three GUI-loop failures involving
sandbox PID inspection, missing-run wording and a missing `cve_patch_pack`
fixture. The wider tool-live run passed 98/100 checks, with a sandbox stop-status
failure and the same stale missing-run wording assertion. These are not a claim
that the entire repository test suite is green.

Private transcripts, terminal JSON, requested-route provenance and the plan are
retained under `/private/tmp/refactory-discovery-acceptance-20260927`; graph
artifacts remain in this worktree's `.factory/discovery-acceptance-20260927`.
The owned server on port 60213 was stopped after acceptance; the worker had
already completed, and its owned Chrome tab was closed. The temporary project file was copied to evidence and removed.
No old run was resumed, credential contents were published, or original tracked
checkout was modified.

# Capability and documentation discovery

The CEO receives a compact [operating guide](ceo-guide.md) through its tool's
system prompt. `refactory help` returns that guide, current operation/mode IDs,
interface support and build/documentation identity. `--topic <ID>` reads actual
argument schemas and examples. Chat uses actions `help`, `docs`, `profiles`,
`profile-resolve` and `workers`; the native panel uses the same mode declarations.

```sh
refactory help
refactory help --topic counting_pack/fixed_step
refactory docs --query 'worker routing'
refactory docs --page refactory/docs/worker-routing.md --limit 6000
```

Docs return exact indexed page IDs, section IDs, resolved links and continuation
offsets. Reads are limited to 12,000 characters; search returns at most 12 bounded
excerpts. Only README and the public `refactory/docs` Markdown tree are bundled.
Runtime retrieval reads the installation's bundle, never project files, private
runs, credentials, swap files or arbitrary paths. Non-document links are identified
as repository assets. Shell/coding/web permissions of the CEO stay restricted.

Coverage targets shipped mode declarations and public console/CLI entry points.
Internal Python helpers are covered by the separate API reference generator,
not advertised as chat actions. Forwarding entry points such as `package` expose
their wrapper schema and supported terminal route; backend-native credential and
configuration flags remain owned by the native product and are deliberately not
chat configuration arguments.

The authoritative facts come from `console._parser()`, the CLI parser, profile
settings, worker capabilities, mode declarations and the installed package
registry. The generated chat schema and invocation mappings use those same
arguments. Interface declarations distinguish callable actions, `wf_open`,
terminal/panel routes and deliberately unavailable configuration controls. Worker
routing is a file/CLI/panel feature with read-only chat discovery.

`refactory_dsh/data/coverage.json` owns reviewed purpose, examples, documentation
links and interface routes. Its `reviewed_schema` binds that guidance to actual
public arguments, defaults and mode structure. Missing/stale metadata fails the
ordinary build with the capability ID, the behavior the CEO cannot reliably
choose/use, and repair instructions. Generation never updates semantic review
hashes automatically. Signatures are facts, not proof that an explanation works.

```sh
pnpm run docs:generate
pnpm run docs:check
pnpm run build
```

Generation is deterministic and offline: no model, credentials, network service
or vector database. It reuses the API reference generator and writes the full
installation docs bundle, [capability reference](api/capabilities.md), and the
TypeScript tool contract. Check mode fails stale artifacts and invalid links.
The build runs check mode first, so it cannot silently repair stale committed
artifacts. Build identity hashes version, schemas, reviewed metadata and docs;
documentation identity hashes indexed pages. Live mode schemas may differ after
installing a package; the help response shows coverage warnings in that case.

## Worked extension: mode

Register a mode normally and declare a new knob with its type, default, bounds
or accepted values, and a useful description. For example, add a frozen input
`target` and an integer `step` to a counting mode. The live catalogue immediately
shows these facts and its nodes/roles/gates/ports. Add a `modes` entry in
`data/coverage.json` explaining when to choose it, a working example such as
`{"knobs":{"target":5,"step":1},"explanation":"Reach five exactly."}`, its
public documentation page and CLI/chat/panel routes. Run `docs:generate` to get
the expected schema hash, review the guidance, and set `reviewed_schema` to that
hash. Regenerate and check. A later knob or graph change produces a new review
diagnostic. Newly installed modes still appear at runtime even without this
metadata, with a visible warning instead of a false claim of complete coverage.

## Worked extension: operation

Add the actual console parser and dispatch implementation, then add its operation
coverage entry: purpose, `examples` with console argument names, `doc`, and all
three interface routes. If it is a CEO action, `chat.fields` maps tool argument
names to actual parser destinations. The generator derives types, flags and
positionals, and the tool uses those mappings to invoke the console. Missing
required mappings and invalid example arguments fail generation. If it is file
or terminal only, omit `chat` and explain the supported route and why chat cannot
mutate it. `workers` and [project worker configuration](worker-routing.md) are a
worked example of intentionally read-only conversational support.

Run focused schema, negative coverage, docs retrieval and invocation tests. For
an exposed model workflow, demonstrate a small actual CEO discovery/docs/launch
case; deterministic schema checks alone do not establish model usability.

refactory/docs/getting-started.md.text:
# Get started

Start with a small offline search, then connect a model for authoring and interactive work. Run commands from the repository root.

## 1. Install

You need Git, [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) `^22.19` or `>=24`, and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). The installer sets up the pinned Node dependencies, Python environment, UI bundles and DSH graph profile.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/boston-harness-group/refactory-dsh.git
cd refactory-dsh
./install.sh
uv run refactory list
```

The repository must be accessible to your GitHub account. `uv` manages the Python environment. Run `./install.sh` again after every pull, then restart any running GUI; see [Updating](../../README.md#updating).

> **Multiple checkouts.** The DSH graph profile links to whichever checkout
> last ran `install.sh`. A run from a different checkout (a second clone, a
> worktree, a contributor's branch) will refuse and name the command that
> relinks the profile. Run `install.sh` from the checkout you want to use, or
> run the named `dsh plugin --profile graph add` command it prints.
>
> **Pinned runs.** When a run is resumed after the driver moved to a new
> commit, a pin is created: a `graph-pin-<commit12>` profile in your own
> `$DSH_HOME` (`~/.dsh` unless you set it), pointing to a prepared worktree of
> the original commit. Your credentials stay in `$DSH_HOME`, which is unchanged.
> `refactory pin list` shows active pins; `refactory pin prune` removes unused ones.

### Builds and restarts

A workspace-wide build stamp covers all TypeScript packages the runtime loads.
At launch, `require_build()` compares the stamp against the current source. When
the build is stale:

- **CLI** (`refactory ceo`, `refactory optimize`): the launcher automatically runs
  `pnpm run build` before starting the run, unless a live run uses the same
  checkout — in that case it warns and continues on the existing build.  When the
  rebuild itself fails (e.g. a syntax error in a TS source), the launch continues
  with a warning naming the stale packages and the command to rebuild manually.
- **GUI** (`refactory ui`): a stale build logs a warning naming the stale packages
  and the command to rebuild (`pnpm run build`).  The GUI does not rebuild `lib/`
  underneath itself.

After every `git pull`, run `./install.sh` and restart any running GUI.

## 2. Try a search without a model

The shipped circle-packing example is deterministic. These options keep proposal generation and evaluation offline:

```bash
uv run refactory optimize circle_packing/adaptive \
  --optimizer random --preset knob_only --evaluator walker \
  --epochs 2 --batch-size 4 --max-evaluations 8 --seed 5 \
  --runs-root .factory/loop/first-search
uv run refactory leaderboard --run .factory/loop/first-search
uv run refactory best --run .factory/loop/first-search
```

Read the candidate changes, raw score and adjusted score. The latter includes the graph-size penalty. This mode has no dataset split, so its holdout is explicitly not applicable. Use a fresh run directory for a separate experiment.

Keep the winner as a new package:

```bash
uv run refactory adopt --run .factory/loop/first-search --as first_tuned
uv run refactory package verify first_tuned
uv run refactory package smoke first_tuned/adaptive
```

Use another package name if `first_tuned` already exists. Adoption preserves the original package.

## 3. Open the GUI and configure a model

```bash
uv run refactory ui --port 3081 --no-open
```

Open the exact URL printed by the server, including its token (`http://127.0.0.1:3081/?token=…`); `--no-open` only stops it from opening a browser itself. Choose this checkout as the workspace, then create a new session. A blank session can open the right sidebar's **Modes** tab; no introductory model message is needed.

In **Settings → Models**, configure a provider and save its API key with **Edit → API key → Apply**. Use the managed credential store for nested authoring and validation. An exported key or a repository `.env` alone does not survive nested execution's secret scrub. See [model setup](models.md#credentials-for-nested-execution).

```bash
uv run refactory doctor
uv run refactory runtime
```

Doctor checks the chosen provider's local configuration, not authentication or quota. Choosing a model in **Settings → Models** (or with `uv run refactory model set --provider <provider> --model <model>`) is the one choice every terminal run uses, and a GUI session starts on it; a terminal run with none uses the only provider with a key and says so, asks at a terminal when several have keys, or is refused ([First run](models.md#first-run)). CLI runs choose their model with `--provider` and `--model` for one run instead; `uv run refactory runtime` shows the route a run would use and where it came from.

New coding workers default to **Skip permission checks**, including full native sandbox bypass for DSH/Codex. Their tools can access what your OS account can access. To retain backend checks, choose **Native permission policy** in the Modes panel or pass `--permission-mode default` in the CLI. Existing saved profiles and runs preserve their policy. [Worker permissions](models.md#model-provider-versus-coding-agent)

## Targets, uncommitted changes and worktrees

A Design run works on the repository its `target` knob names (or a new project when empty). Pass `--target /path/to/repo` in the CLI, or pick one from the GUI's target selector, which lists the same projects as `refactory projects`.

To start a run from your uncommitted changes, set `--knob include_uncommitted=true`. The run copies your modified, staged and untracked files into its worktree and commits them as its own base. Your checkout is never changed.

**Which modes get a worktree:** Design and design_fast use a git worktree. Create, create_fast, edit and edit_fast stage their package in a per-run directory (not a git worktree, because `.factory/` is gitignored). Loop and optimize write only into their run directory and need no isolation.

## 4. Choose the output you want

| Your goal | Use | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Build a reusable workflow | Create | A registered package of modes |
| Revise an existing workflow | Edit | A new package with provenance and comparison status |
| Build software or another artifact | Design | An artifact checked against the supplied command and brief |
| Use a workflow you already have | Run its mode | Its declared outputs and execution evidence |
| Improve a scored workflow | Optimize | Candidate comparisons, audit and a winner eligible for adoption |

Start an interactive terminal run:

```bash
uv run refactory ceo counting_pack/fixed_step \
  --knob target=8 --knob step=2 --intent "Count to eight and explain the recorded result."
```

The knobs supply the operation's inputs; prose intent does not change deterministic inputs automatically. The conversational CEO uses a model even when the underlying mode is deterministic.

To author a small artifact:

```bash
uv run refactory ceo \
  "Build wordcount.py, which prints a file's line, word and character counts as wc -l -w -m counts them, as three numbers separated by spaces, and a plain-ASCII sample.txt." \
  --mode design --name wordcount \
  --check 'test "$(python wordcount.py sample.txt)" = "$(wc -l -w -m < sample.txt | xargs)"'
```

Review the proposed design when asked. The check compares the script's counts with `wc`, so it fails when they are wrong, not only when the script crashes; a check that only runs the script would pass on wrong counts. Still read the check evidence and review findings.

Once the reviews pass, the run opens a pull request, which needs `gh` logged in (`gh auth login`). Without a login the files stay on the run's branch, which the run names (a new project's `main` stays empty), and `delivery.json` in the run directory lists the commands that publish them. Authoring can take substantial time because the current default modes include research and review stages.

To author a reusable mode, follow [Create and Edit](tutorials/03-author-with-a-model.md). Choose a [Task](datasets.md) for repeated items, or `--single` explicitly for a one-off harness.

## 5. Stay involved

In GUI chat, ask: “Open counting_pack/fixed_step with target=8 and step=2. Walk it one node at a time.” Ask to pause before a node, correct an instruction, or answer a gate. In the Modes panel, choose a mode and set its knobs: **Run once** executes it, including full and fast authoring modes; **Start** optimizes a scored mode. Chat supports stepwise authoring and user gates. Fast authoring uses smaller graphs with focused QA and bounded repair; see its [tested scope and resource choices](budgets-fast-modes.md#acceptance-status).

Attach the run's exact directory with **Existing run directory → Read this run** to follow persisted live activity, worker receipts and pending questions. Reading a run does not execute it. Use **resume** explicitly for a supported saved boundary after its owner stops; completed work and consumed resources are retained. [Interface guide](interfaces.md) explains what is interactive, what updates automatically, and when controls take effect.

Next: [command reference](cli.md) · [optimization tutorial](tutorials/02-optimize-it.md) · [write your own mode](tutorials/01-write-a-mode.md).

refactory/docs/hardening.md.text:
# Hardening: what the audit found, and what holds it now

## Failure digest, feedback re-fill and builder probe (dm-120, dm-121)

### The failure digest

Before this change, the builder received raw check output — up to 500 lines of
stack traces, passing-test lines and source-map noise — or, after a redo, the
literal `{{validation}}` placeholder unfilled.

The **failure digest** (`check_digest.py`) parses check output per runner (pytest,
vitest and node's test runner; unknown runners fall back to the raw tail).  Each
failing test's id, assertion or error message and a short traceback are extracted,
with ANSI codes, passing-test lines and source-map warnings stripped.  The digest
is stored in `check-record.json`, which is a file (not a fact) and therefore
survives a redo or rerun.

### Feedback re-fill

Each builder's emit node declares its feedback keys as a `Node.feedback_keys`
field.  Before rendering, `agent_delivery.fill_feedback` — called at the three
render sites (worker_node, nn/executor, agent_delivery.main) — checks whether any
declared key is absent from the facts.  When one is:

1. Re-derive from the producing gate's persisted file (`check-record.json`,
   `validation.txt`, `reviews/qa-gate.txt`, `reviews/overwatch-gate.txt`,
   `repair.txt`).
2. Fall back to `feedback-initial.json` (prepare-time recorded values).
3. Refuse only when both are missing.

The re-fill is resolved through the `refactory.feedback_refill` entry-point group,
following the same pattern as `refactory.environment_overlay`.  Core modules
(`agent_delivery`, `worker_node`, `nn.executor`) import nothing from the product;
they reach the refill logic only through the entry point.

### Agent workspaces

An agent node can declare where it works: `workspace` on the node (`nn.graph`,
saved only when it is not the default, `none`), carried by the IR, the run's
declarations and the worker spec. `scratch` is a fresh empty folder per dispatch;
`clone` (`of: attempt` or `base`) is a prepared clone of the run's worktree.
`collect: files` copies the node's declared writes out of the workspace;
`collect: diff` writes the clone's diff into the node's first write. Both runtimes
run it through one module, `refactory_dsh/workspace.py`: the spine's worker
(`worker_node.execute`) and the walker (`Executor._visit_agent`) prepare the
workspace before the delivery bracket opens and collect from it before it closes, so
`agent_delivery.finish` checks what the workspace produced. A workspace is refused on
the CEO-subagent route (`workers.lower_workflow` with no worker model context): nothing
there could give the node a workspace or collect from it. The spine only passes the
declaration through.

Design mode's builder (`emit`, in design and design_fast) works in a clone of the
last attempt and collects its diff: it edits the repository there, runs the tests its
change touches (the test files it changed or added, and the tests importing the modules
it changed) and the brief's own example or CLI path as often as it needs, and stops. Its
prompt gives it the targeted command the last self-check ran (the check's options kept) and
the seconds that self-check measured for it, and says the full check runs after it answers,
so it does not run the whole suite itself: in the live trial (dm-149) its full-suite runs
took 11.6 of its 27 minutes, and in design runs A1 and A2 its whole-suite runs under its own
`timeout` were killed with no output, up to nine times a session. Materialise,
the check, the reviews and the target guard read the derived `emit.txt` as they read
an emitted one. create, edit and fast-create keep the emission-only builder.

- **Prepared once per run.** The clone (`clones.prepare`, the product's half,
  reached through the `refactory.workspace_clone` entry point) shares the target's
  objects (`git clone --shared`), keeps its own refs and index, and has no remote and
  no hooks. It persists across commands, fix-ups and attempts. When materialise has
  committed what it derived, the clone already holds the new head: the next dispatch
  verifies that (the clone's change from the new head, less what its preparation
  made, is empty) and only moves its base (`verified`). A head that did not move keeps
  the clone as the agent left it (`kept`), so a refused emission's work is still there
  to fix; any other head resets the clone to it (`reset`). A file the agent added counts
  as held when its content and mode are the commit's. Installs run again only when a
  dependency manifest or lockfile anywhere in the clone changes
  (`clones.dependency_fingerprint`), setup with them or after a reset, and generate on
  every dispatch. A step that fails does not stop the node: the agent is told, and the
  check runs the same steps. A pending merge from delivery is started in the clone, its
  generated conflicts resolved to main's side as materialise resolves them; a merge the
  agent finished is kept across a refused round, and one materialise gave up is
  dropped, so main's changes never come back as the agent's own.
- **Run.** The model's working directory is the workspace; its receipt and patch stay
  in the run directory (`DshModelClient.complete(cwd=...)`). Its environment is the
  clone's (`worktree.check_environment`): the clone's own `.venv` and
  `node_modules/.bin` first, the run worktree's taken off PATH, and HOME at the
  clone's `.refactory/home`, with pnpm's store, uv's cache and the XDG cache inside it
  (the person's are read-only to it). Its shell is told a DSH home of its own inside the
  workspace (`workers.write_patch`'s `shell-env` row), and its `BASH_ENV` file unsets the
  run's variables (`REFACTORY_*`, `SRF_*`, `VENV_BIN`, `PYTHONPATH`) before each command,
  as the check never has them; the DSH process keeps them for its observer. Its DSH
  sandbox policy is `workspace-write` rooted at the workspace, with approval `never`
  (`workers.permission_patch`), where a DSH runner works here (bubblewrap or Landlock on
  Linux, Seatbelt on macOS; probed once). Where none does, a workspace node on the dsh
  backend is refused, since its shell would have full access while it is asked to install
  and run things, unless `REFACTORY_WORKSPACE_SANDBOX=unconfined` chooses that; the
  dispatch record and a warning then say so. A native backend (codex, Claude Code) runs
  under its own sandbox and keeps the person's HOME, where its CLI finds its login.
- **Collect.** `derive_emission` writes whole-file `===FILE:` and `===DELETE:` blocks
  from `git diff --raw --no-renames <base>` and the untracked files, leaving out
  `.refactory/`, the environments and tool caches, and what the preparation made while
  the agent left it as made. A binary file, a symlink, a mode change, a new executable,
  a submodule, a line the emission would read as a block header, or (without a
  worktree) a deletion is refused, as is a path an emission header cannot carry (with
  whitespace, `=`, a quote, a backtick or a backslash) or one holding a control or hidden
  format character (the same `unprintable_refusal` an emitted block gets, dm-278), a
  file over 50 MB, a change over 200 MB in all, and a workspace with no change: the
  refusal is left beside the emission
  (`.refactory/workspace-refusal.json`, keyed by its digest) and materialise sends it
  back to the builder like any refused emission. Line endings and end-of-file newlines
  are normalised by the blocks, with a warning, and the next dispatch tells the agent
  which files. Only the repository's own ignore rules apply: the clone ignores a
  person's global ignore file.
- **Clean-up.** At the run's end, however it ended: the walker and the DSH evaluator
  (the `refactory.run_end` entry point) and a spine run's owner. A workspace a
  dispatch holds is left.
- **OpenShell (experimental).** On the `openshell` worker backend the same workspace is
  packed (`openshell_backend.pack_workspace`, after the clone takes its own copy of the
  objects it borrowed), the agent (Claude Code, the binary the gateway's provider admits)
  runs inside the sandbox, and the folder comes back (`download_artifacts`) to the same
  collect step (`workspace.sync_back`, which refuses a folder that is not the workspace's
  copy). It has had no live run, so it is refused unless
  `REFACTORY_OPENSHELL_WORKSPACE=1` opts in. Not yet: packing `.venv` and
  `node_modules`, the node's model and usage for `claude -p`, and the remote stop's PID
  path.

### The builder probe

The emit prompt's "do not apply or test your change anywhere", which create, edit
and fast-create still carry, exists because direct edits to the worktree bypass
materialise and the check. The builder probe gave design's builder a safe way to test
before its workspace did; its prompt no longer names it. Since dm-133, the probe is
also available to `design_doc` via `--command` (no `--emission`); the clone
runs at the run's base with `emission=None`, and the same isolation guarantees
apply:

- **Standalone clone** (`clones.clone_shared`, `git clone --shared`): not a linked
  worktree, so no `.git` registration; its own refs and index, the target's objects
  shared.  `origin` removed after clone.
- **Hooks off**: `core.hooksPath=/dev/null`, `LEFTHOOK=0`, `HUSKY=0`.
- **Isolated HOME and DSH_HOME**: per-probe directories under `probe-<id>/`.
- **PATH stripped**: the run worktree's `.venv/bin` and `node_modules/.bin` are
  removed so tools resolve from the clone, not from the run's worktree.
- **Lifecycle**: cold probes are deleted in a `finally` block. Warm probes
  (`--test` via the CLI) are kept on disk between probes for reuse — the clone
  directory survives with `.venv` and `node_modules` intact — and are removed
  by `sweep_warm_clones`: at `materialise`, and at the run's end by the walker
  (`nn.executor.execute`, through the `refactory.run_end` entry point), by the
  owner of a spine run started from the CLI (`interactive.run`) and by the DSH
  evaluator (`dsh_runtime.evaluate_on_dsh`). A run the GUI's DSH server drives
  has no Python owner, so nothing removes a clone it leaves before materialise.
  A clone another probe is using is skipped; one that cannot be removed is
  named in a warning. Leaked cold probes are swept by `sweep_dead_probes`
  (owner PID check).
- **Not an attempt**: no `commit_attempt`, no attempt counter increment.
- **target_guard preserved**: the existing test at `test_design_worktree.py:667`
  continues to pass.  A cold probe is removed before `finish()`; a warm clone
  stays under the run directory's `.refactory/` until materialise or the
  run's end.

#### Why each isolation guarantee exists

| Guarantee | Reason |
|---|---|
| Standalone clone | dm-96: a PR's checks registered 59 worktrees in the target's .git |
| Origin removed | A push from the probe could reach the shared .git |
| Hooks off | pnpm and lefthook rewrite shared hooks (dm-96) |
| Isolated HOME | Tool caches stay out of the worktree's diff |
| PATH stripped | A missing tool from the clone must not resolve into the run's worktree |
| Lifecycle | Cold probes deleted in finally; warm probes reused within the attempt, cleaned by materialise and at run's end; a SIGKILL leaves a warm clone that the next materialise or end-of-run cleanup removes |

- **Vitest mixed-ID routing**: when a probe command includes both bare spec IDs
  (whole files) and structured `file > suite > test` IDs, the named files run
  whole — more tests than strictly asked, never fewer. Splitting into two
  `&&`-joined invocations was rejected because a failing first invocation would
  silently skip the second (the failure class #502 already fixed for the
  self-check's chunks), and `failfast.targeted_prepass` passes bare spec IDs
  as `test_ids`, so the split would reach the self-check.

#### What is not isolated

Installs use the person's real HOME (`worktree.py:1229-1230`), as the check's
installs do.  `~/.npmrc`, `~/.netrc`, uv configuration and keyrings are how most
private indexes sign in.

## The method

For each issue: read its acceptance criteria as written, then write a probe that
would fail if the criterion were unmet, and run it. Grepping for a name proves a

## 1. `check_package` executed generated code in the driver (#23)

**What the issue said.** create-mode writes Python and then something decides
whether it is usable, "which means loading it, which means executing model-written
code". The table named `create_ops.check_package: imports the generated package to
validate it — none — in-process, full access`.

**What the code did.** The docstring said *"A generated package is **never
imported here**"*. The body's tail was:

```python
package = load_fresh(name)              # importlib.import_module
for ops_module in package.ops:
    importlib.import_module(ops_module)  # model code, again
for mode_class in package.modes:
    problems.extend(_check_mode(mode_class))  # constructs the mode
```

Only the *structural* half ran in a subprocess. The semantic half — is the name
right, do the ops import, is the mode constructible, does it satisfy every
validator rule — ran in the driver with full access.

**The fix.**

- `sandbox.verify_sandboxed` now performs the whole check in its subprocess,
  including the package name, each declared ops module, and each mode's
  construction, score, knobs and validator rules.
- `register` and `smoke` needed the manifest only to *name* what was registered and
  which mode to smoke, and were loading the package to get it. They use the new
  `sandbox.describe_package`, which reads it out of process.
- `load_fresh` and `_check_mode` are deleted. No function in the driver loads a
  generated package any more.

**Held by.** `tests/test_create.py`: a test patches `importlib.import_module` to
record any import of the package's module prefix, runs `check_package` to a clean
result, and asserts the recording is empty. A second does the same for
`describe_package`.

**Known limit, stated rather than implied.** `registry.catalogue` and `registry.load`
still import packages to describe them, so *listing* a generated package still runs
it. That is a different boundary from create-mode's validation, and it is not fixed
here.

## 2. Run retention was declared and never applied (#24)

**What the issue said.** `memory(namespace, kind, retention)` where `retention` is
`run`, `project` or `global` — "the difference between a memory that dies with the
run and one that accumulates".

**What the code did.** `MemoryStore.forget_run_scoped` existed, with a docstring
reading *"Called when the run ends"*, and **nothing called it**. So a run-scoped
namespace accumulated exactly like a project one.

The cost is sharper than untidy files. `_evaluate` re-evaluates candidates when a
run resumes, and a run-scoped memory left on disk is read the second time — so a
resumed run would not be the run it resumed.

**A second gap, found while fixing it.** Memory did not cross to DSH **at all**:
`lowering` dropped it and `run.py` built its `RunContext` without a store. A mode
declaring a cross-run prior therefore worked in the walker and silently kept nothing
on the runtime that ships. Nothing reported the difference, because the running
example declares no memory.

**The fix.**

- `Loop._evaluate` forgets in a `finally`, so a crash or a stop applies the policy
  too, not only a clean finish.
- `lowering.write_declarations` carries the mode's memory declarations beside the
  node facts; `lowering.read_memory_declarations` reads them back; and `run.py`
  builds the store from them, with the same roots the walker uses.

**Held by.** `tests/test_declarations.py`: a run-scoped namespace is gone after
`forget_run_scoped`; project and global namespaces survive it; the loop's
`_evaluate` contains the call **and** a `finally`; the declarations survive the
lowering; and the node runner builds a store.

## 3. The strategies recorded their decision instead of applying it (#20)

**What the issue said.** "The deliverable includes all the SRF candidates
implemented on the new API. The abstraction is proven by the ports, not by the tests
for the abstraction."

**What the code did.** Five strategies took their distinguishing branch, counted it,
logged it, and called the ordinary path:

```python
def epoch_step(self, run=None, *, branch="mutate"):
    if branch == "merge": self.merges += 1
    else:                 self.mutations += 1
    run.log(f"branch={branch}")
    return super().epoch_step(run)     # the merge is not a merge
```

`reflective_sampler` stored `last_reflection` and read it nowhere.
`adaptive_meta` computed `meta` and logged it. `research_then_optimize` stored
`research_note` — `grep` found only the two lines that set and logged it.
`staged_curriculum` logged the stage and ran the ordinary step.

Measured, not argued: running all fourteen on identical input, **six produced
byte-identical leaderboards to `default`**.

The tests passed because they asserted the *counter* —
`test_reflective_takes_a_merge_branch_and_a_mutate_branch` checks
`loop.merges >= 1` — and a branch that changes nothing still increments a counter.

**The fix.** `ProposalContext.strategy` is a new channel carrying what the outer
loop decided for this iteration, so a decision reaches the proposer instead of only
the log. Each strategy now acts:

| strategy | what it now does |
|---|---|
| `adaptive_meta` | widens the batch by 2 on a stall — a real budget decision |
| `reflective` | builds a genuine merge: one parent's knobs taken from another, and it falls back to a mutation when the parents differ structurally rather than in their settings, because a no-op merge is refused as `E-noop` and loses the slot |
| `reflective_sampler` | drops a proposal that repeats an edit the run already refused |
| `research_then_optimize` | publishes its conclusion into the context |
| `staged_curriculum` | publishes which stage is running |

**Held by.** Six tests that assert the **effect**: the batch is wider, the merged
proposal takes the other parent's setting, a refused edit is not re-proposed, and
the decision is present in the context a proposer receives.

**Honest limit.** With `optimizer=random` the model-facing decisions (a research
note, a curriculum stage) reach a proposer that cannot read them, so four strategies
still match `default` on the tiny example. The channel is real; showing the
difference needs a model proposer.

## 4. A revision recorded a name, not a state (#13)

**What the issue said.** Provenance of *"what it was edited from, **at which
state**"*.

**What the code did.** `_revision_source` correctly handed the model the source
files. The record then said `revision_of: "circle_packing/adaptive"` and nothing
else. A mode is not a fixed thing — the outer loop edits it — so that names a class
which may have changed since, and the revision cannot be reproduced or diffed
against what it actually started from.

**The fix.** `edit()` resolves the source mode once, records its whole
`revision_of_state` plus a `revision_of_digest` (the same `candidate_id` the loop
uses, so a revision and a candidate that are the same state agree), and returns the
digest.

**Held by.** A test that runs a revision, reads the origin file, asserts the
recorded state is a full state dict, and that the digest matches both the result and
`candidate_id(state)`.

## 5. The lowering dropped `callable_name` (#21)

**What the issue said.** *"`FnNode.callable_name` already exists; do not invent a
command string."*

**What the code did.** Emitted `command: "python -m refactory_dsh.run <mod>:<fn>"`
and left `callable_name` unset. `callable_name` and `post_checks` appeared zero
times in `lowering.py`.

**Where the issue was right, and where it was wrong.** `callable_name` *is* a real
`FnNode` field — `factory/workflow/primitives.py`, round-tripped by
`factory/workflow/parity.py` — so the lowering was dropping something the language
has. But **DSH's spine does not model it**: `WorkflowNode` has `command`,
`evaluator_type` and `evaluator_command`, and `callable_name` appears nowhere in the
spine's source, which executes the command. A graph carrying only `callable_name`
would be a graph whose nodes never run.

**The fix.** The lowering emits **both**: `callable_name`, so the IR stays faithful
to the language and refactory's own tooling can read it, and `command`, because that
is what the runtime we ship executes.

**Held by.** Two tests: every op node carries both fields, and every declared
`callable_name` resolves.

**Not adopted, stated rather than skipped.** `AgentNode.post_checks` and refactory's
`ForkNode`/`JoinNode` are still unused. `post_checks` would duplicate a check the
executor already performs; adopting fork/join is a real design change, not a
fidelity fix, and is not done. Design's `emit` still needs none: an `emit.txt`
`materialise` cannot apply is sent back to `emit` by the check (#361).

## 6. The documented commands, run as written (#31)

Ship readiness is not a feeling about the code; it is the claim that a person who has
never seen this repository can install it, follow the docs, and get the promised
result. That claim is testable, so it is a test: `tests/test_ship_ready.py` reads the
shipped documents, extracts every command line from their `bash` blocks, and runs it.

The gate checks four things, and each one found something:

| check | what it would catch |
|---|---|
| every `python -m refactory_dsh.X` a doc names imports | a tutorial pointing at a deleted module |
| every module's `--help` accepts the flags the doc shows | a flag renamed in code but not in the prose |
| the README links the architecture and the tutorials | a stranger with nowhere to go next |
| the docs the README promises exist on disk | a link to a file that was moved |

**The bug it found.** `python -m refactory_dsh.sandbox --help` printed its usage line
to **stderr** and exited **2**. Two things were wrong with that, and the second is the
worse one: a reader who asks for help is told they made an error, and a program that
captures stdout — which is how the doc gate itself reads a help page — saw nothing at
all. So the flag table was empty and the gate could not check the sandbox CLI, which
is where an unknown flag had to be caught by hand.

**The fix.** `sandbox.main` gained `usage()`, which is the one string both paths
print, and an explicit branch: `-h`/`--help` prints it to **stdout** and returns
**0**. The two cases that are genuinely misuse keep their old behaviour, because they
are a different decision and were already deliberate:

| invocation | stream | status | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-h`, `--help` | stdout | 0 | a question, answered |
| no arguments | stderr | 2 | nothing was asked for; `test_the_sandbox_cli_needs_an_instruction` pins this |
| an unknown flag | stderr | 2 | not a command |

**Held by.** A test that runs `--help` against `sandbox`, `loop` and `console` and
requires both a zero status and non-empty stdout. It is not vacuous: the pre-fix
behaviour (status 2, empty stdout) fails exactly that assertion, which was run both
ways when the fix was made.

**The second finding was in the README, not the code.** It described the layout but
never linked `docs/architecture.md` or `docs/tutorials/`, so the entry point a
stranger actually opens did not lead anywhere. The README now carries a Documentation
table — architecture, tutorials, API, tool packing, hardening, contributing.

**Also regenerated.** `docs/api/reference.md` is generated from the code and had
drifted from it; the new `usage()` export made that visible. `test_docs_api.py` fails
when the two disagree, so the reference is checked rather than trusted.

**And the tracker's own commit field was not checked.** The gate asked a done item for
a non-empty `commit`, which `"(pending)"` satisfies, so six closed items carried one
and the field proved nothing. A recorded commit exists so a reader can go and look at
the change; `test_a_recorded_commit_is_one_git_actually_knows` now runs `git cat-file
-e` on every one, and all 23 done items resolve. Verified both ways: planting a
made-up hash fails the gate, and removing it passes.

**The install itself was run, not inferred.** `./install.sh` is the one command a
stranger executes, and everything above only proves the commands *after* it work. It
was run against this checkout: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `pnpm run build`,
the venv, the editable installs, and the registry listing all
completed with status 0. The build was then checked for the damage a build can do —
`git status` is clean, the Python suite is unchanged, the DSH-side specs pass, and the
doc gates pass — because "it exited 0" and "it left the tree working" are different
claims and only the second one matters.

**What this still does not prove.** It is not a clean clone: the venv already existed,
so the script's fresh-clone branches were not exercised. A machine with neither was not available here.
